title: How do we get there?
goal: Ride anything in Taiwan and explain the route — using the 從…到… pattern and putting the means of transport in the right place: before the verb.
bekal: choose between 坐, 搭, 騎, and 開 for each vehicle
use 從…到… to name the starting point and the destination
ask about routes and travel time

notes: ⚠️ **機車 in Taiwan means a motor scooter**, and Taiwan has one of the highest scooter densities in the world — about fourteen million for twenty-three million people. ⚠️ In young people's slang, 機車 also means "annoying, difficult": *他很機車* (he's such a pain).
**慢慢來 ("take it slow") is one of the most typically Taiwanese words of encouragement.** It's said to anyone who is learning, nervous, or in a rush. You'll hear it often, and it really is soothing.

**億 (*yì*) means a hundred million.** Mandarin has its own big units: 萬 (ten thousand), 億 (a hundred million). A hundred million isn't "a hundred millions" but one 億 — and English big numbers, grouped in thousands, often need recalculating.
⚠️ **不熟 ("not familiar") is used for places, people, and skills.** *我對台北還不熟* (I don't know Taipei well yet), *我跟他不熟* (I don't know him well). A very useful word that's rarely taught.
**紅線, 藍線, 綠線** — Taipei MRT lines are known by color, not number. The map at every station uses colors, and people name them that way when giving directions.

grammars.title: 坐, 搭, 騎, 開: choosing the verb for each vehicle
body: English switches between "take", "ride", and "drive". Mandarin also picks the verb by **how you sit on or in the vehicle**.

head: Verb
Pīnyīn
Used for
Example
rows: sitting inside: bus, train, plane, taxi
same as 坐, slightly more refined

after: ⚠️ **騎 is used for anything you straddle** — scooter, bicycle, horse. Using 坐 for a scooter sounds odd, like saying "sit a bicycle" in English.
**The means of transport stands BEFORE the verb of going**: *我坐捷運去學校* — "I take the MRT to campus". It's the same rule as for time and place: all adverbials come before the main verb.
**開 also means "open" and "switch on"**: 開門 (open the door), 開燈 (turn on the light), 開會 (have a meeting), 開始 (begin). The same character, a wide family of meanings.

grammars.title: 從…到…: from where to where, and how long
body: **從 A 到 B** is the frame used for distance, time, and sequence alike. Both parts stand **before the verb**, like every other adverbial.

head: Sentence
Pīnyīn
Meaning
rows: Cóng Táiběi dào Táinán yào liǎng xiǎoshí.
Taipei to Tainan takes two hours.
cóng jiǔ diǎn dào wǔ diǎn
Where are you from / coming from?

after: ⚠️ **要 here means "need, take (time)"**, not "want": *要兩小時* = "takes two hours". This meaning shows up whenever 要 is followed by an amount of time or money: *要多少錢？* (needs how much money = how much is it).
**Asking about travel time: 要多久？** (*yào duō jiǔ?*) — "how long does it take?". The answer uses a time unit placed after the verb: *要半個小時* (takes half an hour).

blocks.title: Taiwan's trains: two different systems
items: **高鐵 (HSR)** — high-speed rail along the west coast, Taipei–Kaohsiung in about 1 hour 45 minutes. Pricey, fast, stations on the edge of town.
**台鐵 (TRA)** — the regular railway circling the whole island, including the east coast to 花蓮 and 台東. Cheaper, slower, stations in the city center.
⚠️ **For 花蓮 and 台東, the only train is 台鐵** — 高鐵 doesn't run along the east coast at all.
**台鐵 classes:** 自強號 (fastest), 莒光號, 區間車 (stops everywhere). Book through the app or at a 便利商店.
**悠遊卡 works on the 捷運, 公車, YouBike, and short 台鐵 trips** — but not on the 高鐵.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **上車 and 下車 mean getting on and off a vehicle**, using the same 上/下 pair as 上課/下課 and 上班/下班. And **麻煩** (*máfán*, "trouble") opens a very polite request: *麻煩你* = "sorry to trouble you, could you…".

**塞車 ("blocked vehicles") means a traffic jam**, and Taipei flows far better than many big Asian cities — but try leaving town during a 連假 and you'll use this word again and again. To predict one: *可能會塞車* ("there might be traffic").
